rv.q: Quilter is certainly not the first to explore the mental frailties of ageing on stage — he’s also not the first to use the empathy at the heart of drama to draw the audience into the world as the protagonist sees it (Florian Zeller’s The Father is a heartbreaking example). But his approach is to match style to subject.
It offers plenty of laughs, and shows that Lipman has lost none of her stage charisma.
Allegra presents like one of Alan Bennett's lovable, spirited eccentrics, but we learn nothing about her beyond her unworldliness.
She also deserves to be in a better play.
Yet, theatrically, it’s still pedestrian fare of a clumping kind.
This remains a joyous and memorable evening of theatre.
Her joyous performance captivates from the opening moments and never loosens its grip.
Lipman is a delight to watch in this nostalgic and touching play.
But in between these gaudy joyful tent-poles the structure sags dreadfully.

cn.t: Lipman shines at 80 in this lightweight comedy about a singing eccentric, but critics are divided on Quilter's script—some find it witty and heartwarming, while others deem it sluggish and sitcom-like, lacking the quirky accomplishment of their previous collaboration.
